content: The systematic review evaluated the effects, safety, and acceptability of compact, prefilled auto-disable devices (CPADs) when used by lay health workers. It also analyzed large-scale programs aimed at scaling up human resources for health in lowand middle-income countries (LMICs). Additionally, it reviewed barriers and facilitators to the effectiveness and implementation of doctor-nurse substitution programs and examined stakeholder views on optimizing the roles of healthcare providers for maternal and newborn health in LMICs. The analysis included data from the HIFA 2015 email archive. The authors of the reviews and studies engaged in a series of face-to-face and online discussions to identify common implementation factors across task-shifting programs, as well as factors specific to particular program types. Multiple iterations of the analysis were developed based on feedback and discussions. Evidence on the effectiveness of interventions delivered by specific health workers was extracted systematically. Up-to-date review documents and data were obtained from review authors or the Cochrane Library. Relevant analyses were selected for critical comparisons and outcomes, while irrelevant ones were excluded. The GRADE assessment criteria were applied to evaluate the certainty of the evidence (or quality of evidence) for each outcome. This process determined whether the evidence could support specific recommendations. The certainty of evidence was categorized as high, moderate, low, or very low, based on predefined criteria. Rankings could be downgraded for serious risks of bias, inconsistency across studies, or publication bias. Conversely, rankings could be upgraded for very large effect sizes or dose-response relationships. GRADE Profiler software was used for quantitative meta-analyses, and GRADE evidence profiles (or summary of findings tables) were prepared for each comparison. These profiles summarized the evidence and were included in Annex 7. Full reviews on which the GRADE evidence profiles were based were not included in the document but were available upon request. Systematic reviews of qualitative studies explored factors affecting the implementation of programs to optimize health worker roles. Key findings were identified, and the certainty of evidence for each finding was assessed. High-certainty findings were consistent across diverse settings or had convincing explanations for variations. Moderate-certainty findings were less consistent or based on lower-quality studies. Low-certainty findings were inconsistent and lacked convincing explanations for variations. The evidence was presented using the DECIDE evidence-to-recommendations framework, which supports informed decision-making. This framework helped the Guidance Panel evaluate the pros and cons of complex options and provided a structured format for key factors, judgments, research evidence, and comments. For each guidance question, the framework included judgments on the balance of desirable and undesirable consequences, recommendations, justifications, implementation considerations, and monitoring and evaluation priorities. The Guidance Panel finalized recommendations during two technical consultations. The first consultation addressed all recommendations except those related to contraceptives, which were completed in the second consultation. Recommendations on antiretroviral initiation and maintenance for preventing mother-to-child transmission of HIV were removed to align with updated WHO guidelines. Participants in the consultations discussed evidence summarized in the evidence-to-recommendation framework and revised recommendations as needed. In some cases, interventions were separated or health worker categories were further divided for clarity. For example, associate clinicians were split into advanced-level associate clinicians and associate clinicians with lower training levels. Similarly, auxiliary nurses were divided into auxiliary nurses and auxiliary nurse midwives. The Guidance Panel considered evidence on the benefits and harms of interventions, resource use, acceptability, and feasibility. Decisions were made by consensus or, if necessary, by voting. Strong disagreements were recorded, and unresolved issues were put to a vote. WHO staff, external technical experts, and observers did not vote. Participants with academic conflicts of interest could discuss but not vote on related issues. The WHO required all experts to declare competing interests before attending meetings. Declaration of Interest Forms were reviewed by the WHO Secretariat, and verbal declarations were made at the start of meetings. Procedures for managing conflicts of interest were followed, and the participation of all Guidance Panel members was deemed appropriate.
